newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU adopts tightening of wild species trade rules.
newsitem.headline: EU adopts tightening of wild species trade rules.

text.p: The Environment Council adopted a new regulation on Monday to tighten controls on the multi-billion-dollar EU trade in endangered animal and plant species such as rhinoceros, tigers, parrots and orchids.

The new rule, replacing Council Regulation 3626/82, is intended to adapt control and monitoring measures for wildlife traded in the Community to take account of the looser border controls in force since the single market came into force.

"As one of the world's major consumers of wildlife and wildlife products, the EU must take its responsibilities for ensuring trade is at sustainable levels," European Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjjerregaard told a news conference.
The Council's decision updates the EU's implementation of promises made within the 134-country Convention on Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).

The move will introduce mandatory sanctions for wildlife traffickers caught by EU member state authorities and the creation of EU-level bodies to monitor and coordinate enforcement. It will also provide for controls on trade in wildlife species not covered by CITES, an accompanying European Commission statement said.
Environmental campaign group World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) said the law was "one of the world's toughest" for a trade second only to habitat loss as a cause of species extinction.

"EU member states now have to implement the law without delay," WWF policy director Gordon Shepherd told the same news conference, adding that world wildlife trade was worth $50 billion a year excluding timber and all fisheries products.
Shepherd said the EU captured one third of the world market and that one quarter of all the trade was illegal.

The Commission and WWF pledged to spend 900,000 European currency units between them in the coming months to raise awareness of the new rules among airlines, airport authorities, travel agents and tourists.
